course_details.Overview of class:
Thinking Globally

This course examines the impact and implications of today's dynamic international context for nations, communities, and individuals, and equips students with core analytical tools for understanding how global forces shape everyday life. To operate thoughtfully in a global context, citizens, corporations, and governments must understand other cultures and political-economic systems and how global processes influence domestic activities. This course develops that capacity through interdisciplinary social scientific inquiry grounded in geography, history, and material analysis. Framed as an introduction to global thinking, the course cultivates key intellectual habits central to International Studies: attention to scale (local, regional, and global), spatial awareness and geography, historical depth, and the material effects of global processes on lived environments. Students learn to analyze contemporary global phenomena (e.g. climate change, urbanization, empire, conspiracy cultures, or protectionism) by situating them within longer historical trajectories and spatially uneven global systems.


The course is co-taught by two International Studies faculty and structured around collaborative inquiry. Students work in groups on a sustained research project examining a global commodity system, investigating the historical, geographical, institutional, and environmental relationships that organize its production, circulation, and consumption. Organized around four habits of global thinking—time, space, scale, and futures—the project asks students to investigate how commodity systems emerge historically, connect distant places, operate through institutions at different scales, and might be transformed toward more socially just and ecologically sustainable futures. Through a series of cumulative assignments involving historical research, spatial mapping, institutional analysis, and future-oriented inquiry, students develop a coherent understanding of how global economic systems produce uneven social, economic, and environmental consequences. These collaborative assignments culminate in an integrated research portfolio and final presentation.

This year, the course will focus on ‘degrowth' as a critical lens in international studies. Thinking globally about degrowth will enable students to explore and more deeply understand the intersections of economic history, policy, justice, and global conflict and cooperation.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
1. Analyze reciprocal relationships between global systems and human action by examining how economic, environmental, and political processes connect distant places and shape local experiences, livelihoods, and decision-making. Through the study of global commodity systems, students will investigate how production, circulation, and consumption create relationships of interdependence and how individuals, communities, and institutions both shape and respond to these relationships.

2. Demonstrate knowledge of key social science theories related to globalization, political economy, environmental change, and development, and use them to explain how colonialism, capitalism, industrialization, and economic growth have historically structured global relationships. Drawing on scholarship in degrowth studies, environmental history, and political economy, students will critically evaluate how systems of production and consumption generate inequalities in wealth, power, resource access, and environmental consequences.

3. Use appropriate interdisciplinary research methodologies, including historical interpretation, spatial analysis, institutional analysis, and collaborative research, to investigate the organization and consequences of global economic systems. Working in research teams on a sustained global commodity system project, students will reconstruct historical developments, map networks of materials, labor, and capital, and analyze the geographical distribution of economic benefits and environmental burdens. Their findings will be communicated through analytical essays, maps, research memoranda, and collaborative presentations.

4. Critically assess scholarly and policy-oriented arguments concerning economic growth, degrowth, environmental governance, and global inequality by examining their theoretical assumptions, evidentiary foundations, and implications for social and ecological well-being. Through readings and research on global production systems, students will analyze how communities, corporations, national governments, and international institutions exercise power across scales and evaluate the possibilities and limitations of existing approaches to sustainability and resource governance.

5. Evaluate how social science theories and interdisciplinary research can inform responses to contemporary global challenges and the development of alternative futures, particularly those concerning ecological limits, economic inequality, sustainability, and social justice. Building on their historical, spatial, and institutional analyses, students will develop a research-informed vision for transforming their selected global commodity system by 2050, identifying the changes in production, consumption, governance, and labor necessary to advance ecological sustainability and human well-being while considering the political and ethical challenges of such transformations.

A discussion of why we want to "do good"; how to try to do good (and why problems exist in the first place); and, how to know if you did good. Applications to public policy as well as personal life.

course_details.Overview of class:
Elliott Scholars entails a two-course sequence over winter and spring quarters, followed by participation in an international internship opportunity through the Global Engagement Studies Institute (GESI) in the summer quarter.

During GESI, students will engage in internships, joining the efforts of community organizations to advance community-driven change. This hands-on, collaborative experience will provide Elliott Scholars with the opportunity to apply what they have learned throughout the program in a community development setting abroad.

Students must commit to all program components across winter, spring and summer quarters to receive credit. Please note that GESI is non-repeatable, and so GESI alumni are not eligible for this program.

course_details.Topic: A Practitioner's Guide to Diplomatic Craftsmanship
course_details.Overview of class:
A Practitioner's Guide to Diplomatic Craftsmanship

What does it take to stop a war, negotiate the release of hostages, secure humanitarian access, or navigate the competing demands of state and non-state actors?
Drawing on four decades of diplomatic experience, this hands-on seminar takes students inside the high-stakes world of international diplomacy, conflict management, and negotiation. Focusing primarily on the Middle East from 2008 to the present, the course examines real diplomatic challenges involving Israel and Palestine, regional powers including Egypt, Iran, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, and critical international actors such as the United States, Norway, and the United Nations (UN). Through simulations and real-world cases, students will take on the roles of negotiators, Israeli and Palestinian political leaders, UN diplomats, and White House advisers as they confront ceasefires, hostage negotiations, humanitarian crises, Security Council diplomacy, state-building, and war-zone evacuations.
This course will be taught by Tor Wennesland, a veteran Norwegian diplomat and former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process. A Buffett Distinguished Practitioner in Residence during winter 2027, he brings decades of experience in Middle East diplomacy, including service as Norway's Representative to the Palestinian Authority, Ambassador to Egypt and Libya, and Special Envoy to the Middle East.

Critical Perspectives on Territorial Conflict

What distinguishes wars over territory from other types of conflicts? What is the connection between territorial conflict and population transfers between states? How are the lost lands and forced displacement of people remembered and commemorated in the loss-incurring states? In this seminar-style course we will examine these intertwined questions through class discussions and an array of assigned academic articles, book chapters and contemporary and historical case studies of territorial conflicts.

We will begin with canonical accounts of territory's indivisibility and unique value, then study the aftermaths of territorial loss for the geographically "shrunk" states. We then turn to population transfers and ethnic cleansing as well as the resulting changes in ethnic composition of states and the unique nature of displaced co-citizens from the lost territories as a new type of national minority. In the second half of the course, we will study the legacies of territorial conflict through scholarship on the inter-generational transmission of trauma, collective memory and path-dependent analysis of territorial conflict in historical perspective.

In the final two weeks, we will investigate two case studies of territorial conflict-Finland's loss of Karelia in WWII and Armenia's loss of Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023-and the contemporary resurgence of territorial claims in the US foreign policy and beyond.

course_details.Overview of class:
The Refugee in Global Discourse

Since the 1951 UN Convention on the Status of Refugees, the UNHCR has defined a refugee as someone fleeing due to "well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion…" Despite such a definition, however, discourse surrounding the refugee figure remains to be a divided and contentious issue, complicated by other migration categories such as immigrants, asylum seekers, and economic migrants. In this capstone, we will critically analyze scholarship and theory as it relates to the migration of people across borders and explore the myriad constructions of the refugee figure, with particular emphasis on race, class, gender, and sexuality.
By examining refugee resettlement to other migratory patterns, this course foregrounds comparative analysis, with particular emphasis on racial formation, diasporic consciousness, colonial and post-colonial critique, and empire on a global scale.
